title: The second and third time
hook: going once, going twice: some things only settle on the third
tomorrow: a rule you give yourself: is it still a rule?

segments.voice: Yesterday, saranam: refuge, a place you go on good days and bad. I go for refuge. And behind it, a whole week of words: a breath in the word, homage to him, the Blessed One, the worthy one, fully awake. Today they come back as a round, with one small new phrase to hold them.
screen: `I GO FOR REFUGE.` → `A WEEK OF WORDS COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: Going once. Going twice. Sold. Nobody at an auction thinks the first call is enough, and nobody needs it explained: some things only settle on the third. The refuges work in threes too. After the first round, the chant starts again with one new word, dutiyampi, a second time, and then tatiyampi, a third time. So, yesterday's question: why not once?
screen: `GOING ONCE, GOING TWICE.` → `DUTIYAMPI, TATIYAMPI.` → `WHY NOT ONCE?`

segments.voice: Honest answer first: the chant itself never says why. It just does it. Dutiyampi Buddham saranam gacchami: a second time, to the Buddha I go for refuge. Then the dhamma, then the sangha. Then tatiyampi, and all three again. Notice that each round names all three refuges; the three times aren't one per jewel. Where the texts do show the threefold saying at work is the Vinaya, the monks' rule. There, the Buddha allows a newcomer to go forth by saying the refuges this way, three times through. Said once, it's a line. Said three times, in front of others, it marks a real step, like the third call at an auction. And for anyone just learning there is a plainer gift: by the third round, the words come without looking at the sheet. So the second and third time aren't filler. They're how the words become a decision. A second time, a third.
screen: `THE CHANT DOESN'T SAY WHY.` · `EACH ROUND NAMES ALL THREE.` · `IN THE VINAYA: HOW ONE WENT FORTH.` · `A LINE BECOMES A STEP.` · then, large: `A SECOND TIME, A THIRD.`

segments.voice: Chant the refuges three times through, as slowly as you like: Buddham, dhammam, sangham saranam gacchami, then dutiyampi, then tatiyampi. When the third round ends, keep still and listen to the last sound of your own voice fading, all the way to the quiet underneath it.
The second and third time. Dutiyampi, tatiyampi: the words that turn one saying of the refuges into three. Word nine of a little Pali.
screen: `THE SECOND AND THIRD TIME — today's word`.

segments.voice: The line for this one: a second time, a third, and the words become a step. A week and a day of Pali.

screen: `DAY 1435 COUNTS.` → `A LITTLE PALI · 9 OF 29.` → `TOMORROW: A RULE YOU GIVE YOURSELF: IS IT STILL A RULE?`

howItsDone: In Theravada temples the refuges are chanted three times through, with dutiyampi and tatiyampi opening the second and third rounds, usually right after the homage.

options: The chant doesn't say. In the Vinaya, saying them three times is how someone went forth.
Once for each jewel: the Buddha first time, the dhamma second, the sangha third.
Because the Buddha said anything said only once doesn't count at all.
chat.meaning: The chant never explains the three. In the Vinaya, the refuges said three times through are how a newcomer went forth, so the words become a step.

sangha.meaning: the community who practice the Buddha's teaching

Vinaya Mahavagga I.12 (Rhys Davids and Oldenberg, SBE XIII) paraphrased: the Buddha allows going forth (and, at that stage, ordination) by the threefold going for refuge. 'in front of others' summarizes the procedure (head shaved, robes, salutation, then the refuges said three times). Keeper: confirm.
'the chant itself never says why' is deliberate honesty; no reason for the threefold form is invented.
The auction image in the hook is the narrator's illustration.
